steps.label: Do Now: An IF Inside an IF (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: An IF Inside an IF (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the program check the highest number first?Show the answer

A high score also passes the lower check. Checking the highest first means each score gets only the best result it earns.

From 2.3.

1  DECLARE Points : INTEGER
2  INPUT Points
3  IF Points >= 90 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Distinction"
5  ELSE
6      IF Points > 60 THEN
7          OUTPUT "Pass"
8      ELSE
9          OUTPUT "Try again"
10      ENDIF
11  ENDIF
Total: 3 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: an IF inside an IF

steps.text: This is a different program. Do the same steps with your program.
steps.visual:
1  DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
2  INPUT Temp
3  IF Temp >= 35 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Hot"
5  ELSE
6      IF Temp > 25 THEN
7          OUTPUT "Warm"
8      ELSE
9          OUTPUT "Cool"
10      ENDIF
11  ENDIF

steps.text: 35 is input. Line 3: 35 >= 35. >= means more than or equal to. 35 is equal to 35, so it is TRUE. The THEN branch runs and the whole ELSE is skipped.
steps.visual:
1  DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
2  INPUT Temp
3  IF Temp >= 35 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Hot"
5  ELSE
6      IF Temp > 25 THEN
7          OUTPUT "Warm"
8      ELSE
9          OUTPUT "Cool"
10      ENDIF
11  ENDIF
Output: Hot

steps.text: 25 is input. Line 3: 25 >= 35 is FALSE, so go into the ELSE. Line 6: 25 > 25. > means more than, and 25 is not more than 25, so it is FALSE too.
steps.visual:
1  DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
2  INPUT Temp
3  IF Temp >= 35 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Hot"
5  ELSE
6      IF Temp > 25 THEN
7          OUTPUT "Warm"
8      ELSE
9          OUTPUT "Cool"
10      ENDIF
11  ENDIF
Output: Cool

steps.text: The smallest whole number for Warm: try the number in the condition on line 6 first. 25 > 25 is FALSE. The next whole number up is 26, and 26 > 25 is TRUE.
steps.visual:

4      OUTPUT "Hot"
5  ELSE
6      IF Temp > 25 THEN

8      ELSE

steps.label: Do Now: Data Types (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Data Types (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a value that is only ever TRUE or FALSE need its own data type?Show the answer

The computer then knows only two values are allowed, and a condition can use the variable straight away.

From 2.2: data types. The program stops with an error.

1  DECLARE Shop : STRING
2  DECLARE Locked : INTEGER
3  DECLARE Price : REAL
4  Shop <- "Cafe"
5  Locked <- TRUE
6  Price <- 25.5
7  OUTPUT Shop
Total: 2 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: the wrong data type

steps.text: This is a different program. Do the same steps with your program.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Team : INTEGER
DECLARE Goals : INTEGER
Goals <- 3
Team <- "Tigers"
OUTPUT Goals

steps.text: DECLARE does not store anything. It only gives each variable its data type.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Team : INTEGER
DECLARE Goals : INTEGER
Goals <- 3
Team <- "Tigers"
OUTPUT Goals

steps.text: Line 3 stores 3 in Goals. 3 is a whole number and Goals is an INTEGER, so that is fine.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Team : INTEGER
DECLARE Goals : INTEGER
Goals <- 3
Team <- "Tigers"
OUTPUT Goals

steps.text: Line 4 stores "Tigers" in Team. It is in quotes, so it is text. Team was declared as an INTEGER, so the program stops here.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Team : INTEGER
DECLARE Goals : INTEGER
Goals <- 3
Team <- "Tigers"
OUTPUT Goals
Team <- "Tigers": stops here

steps.text: The fix goes on the DECLARE line. Text needs STRING, so line 1 becomes DECLARE Team : STRING. Now do yours: what kind of value is stored?
steps.visual:
DECLARE Team : INTEGER
DECLARE Goals : INTEGER
Goals <- 3
Team <- "Tigers"
OUTPUT Goals

steps.label: 2.4: AND, OR and NOT
steps.content:
Programming, Logic and Testing

2.4: AND, OR and NOT

Year 8

  • Today: about 20 minutes of notes. Then use your notes in Data Bridge.
  • The big question: how can one IF check two rules at once, and why does the word we choose change the answer?
Think → Pair → ShareA theme park ride has two rules: you must be old enough and tall enough. How could a program check both rules?Show the answer

Collect ideas: one IF after another, or one IF that checks both. Today shows a way to join two conditions in one IF.

steps.label: AND: Both Must Be TRUE
steps.content:
AND: Both Must Be TRUE

1  DECLARE Age : INTEGER
2  DECLARE Height : INTEGER
3  INPUT Age
4  INPUT Height
5  IF Age >= 10 AND Height >= 140 THEN
6      OUTPUT "Ride"
7  ELSE
8      OUTPUT "Sorry"
9  ENDIF
AgeHeightAge >= 10Height >= 140Output
12150TRUETRUERide
12130TRUEFALSESorry
8150FALSETRUESorry
8130FALSEFALSESorry
Logical operator: a word that joins two conditions or changes one. AND is the first of three you learn today.
AND: the whole condition is TRUE only when both conditions are TRUE.

WHY? The ride has two rules and both must be kept. So one FALSE is enough to say Sorry.

Think → Pair → ShareA door opens with a key card and the right PIN. Why must the program check both, not just one?Show the answer

Ideas: someone with only a stolen card, or only the PIN, must not get in. Both rules must be kept.

steps.label: Your Notes: AND
steps.content:
Your Notes: AND

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

Logical operator
A word that joins two conditions or changes one. There are three: write the other two when you learn them.
AND
TRUE only when both conditions are TRUE. One FALSE makes the whole condition FALSE.
Example: IF Age >= 10 AND Height >= 140 THEN
How to work it out
Put the values in. Write TRUE or FALSE above each condition first. Then join them.

steps.label: OR: At Least One Must Be TRUE
steps.content:
OR: At Least One Must Be TRUE

The rule: entry is free for children under 5 and for people aged 65 or older.

1  DECLARE Age : INTEGER
2  INPUT Age
3  IF Age < 5 OR Age >= 65 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Free"
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT "Pay"
7  ENDIF
AgeAge < 5Age >= 65Output
3TRUEFALSEFree
30FALSEFALSEPay
70FALSETRUEFree
OR: the whole condition is TRUE when at least one condition is TRUE. It is FALSE only when both are FALSE.

WHY? Each reason is enough on its own to get in free. So one TRUE is enough.

Think → Pair → ShareThe rule says "children under 5 and people aged 65 or older", but the program uses OR. Why is OR right here?Show the answer

Ideas: nobody is under 5 and 65 or older at the same time. Each person needs only one of the two reasons.

steps.label: Your Notes: OR
steps.content:
Your Notes: OR

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

OR
TRUE when at least one condition is TRUE. FALSE only when both are FALSE.
Example: IF Age < 5 OR Age >= 65 THEN
Copy this table
FirstSecondANDOR
TRUETRUETRUETRUE
TRUEFALSEFALSETRUE
FALSETRUEFALSETRUE
FALSEFALSEFALSEFALSE
WHY the rule words can trick you
Read what each person needs. If one reason is enough, use OR, even if the rule says "and".

steps.label: NOT: Change TRUE to FALSE
steps.content:
NOT: Change TRUE to FALSE

Raining is FALSE. Output: Play outside

1  DECLARE Raining : BOOLEAN
2  Raining <- FALSE
3  IF NOT Raining THEN
4      OUTPUT "Play outside"
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT "Play inside"
7  ENDIF

Raining is TRUE. Output: Play inside

1  DECLARE Raining : BOOLEAN
2  Raining <- TRUE
3  IF NOT Raining THEN
4      OUTPUT "Play outside"
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT "Play inside"
7  ENDIF
NOT: changes TRUE to FALSE, and FALSE to TRUE. NOT Raining is TRUE when Raining is FALSE.
AgeNOT Age >= 13Age < 13
12TRUETRUE
13FALSEFALSE
14FALSEFALSE

WHY? NOT with a BOOLEAN variable reads like English: "if not raining". NOT Age >= 13 gives the same answers as Age < 13.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is a BOOLEAN variable a good fit for NOT?Show the answer

Ideas: it is already TRUE or FALSE, so NOT can change it straight away, and the line reads like a sentence.

steps.label: Your Notes: NOT
steps.content:
Your Notes: NOT

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

NOT
Changes TRUE to FALSE, and FALSE to TRUE.
Example: IF NOT Raining THEN runs its THEN branch when Raining is FALSE.
NOT with a comparison
NOT Age >= 13 means the same as Age < 13.
WHY use NOT
A BOOLEAN variable is already TRUE or FALSE. NOT Raining reads like English: "if not raining".

steps.label: Compare: Between Two Numbers
steps.content:
Compare: Between Two Numbers

The rule: a booking accepts 1 to 6 seats. Two programmers wrote line 3 differently.

A: IF Seats >= 1 AND Seats <= 6 THEN

B: IF Seats >= 1 OR Seats <= 6 THEN

Every number is 1 or more, or 6 or less.
SeatsA outputsB outputs
0RejectedAccepted
3AcceptedAccepted
9RejectedAccepted
Range: all the numbers from a lowest value to a highest value, like 1 to 6. A number inside a range needs two conditions joined with AND.

WHY? With OR, one of the two conditions is always TRUE, so B accepts every number. AND needs both, so only 1 to 6 get in.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does testing B with 3 not show the mistake?Show the answer

Ideas: 3 is inside the range, so both programs accept it. Only a number outside the range makes them disagree.

steps.label: Your Notes: Inside a Range
steps.content:
Your Notes: Inside a Range

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

Range
All the numbers from a lowest value to a highest value, like 1 to 6.
Inside a range: AND
IF Seats >= 1 AND Seats <= 6 THEN
The number must be at least the lowest AND at most the highest.
WHY not OR
Every number is 1 or more, or 6 or less, so with OR the condition is always TRUE.

steps.label: Compare: Outside the Range
steps.content:
Compare: Outside the Range

Same rule, 1 to 6 seats. This time line 3 looks for a number outside the range.

A: IF Seats < 1 OR Seats > 6 THEN

B: IF Seats < 1 AND Seats > 6 THEN

1  DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
2  INPUT Seats
3  IF Seats < 1 OR Seats > 6 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Rejected"
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT "Accepted"
7  ENDIF
SeatsA outputsB outputs
0RejectedAccepted
3AcceptedAccepted
9RejectedAccepted
Outside a range: too low OR too high. Either one is enough to reject the number.

WHY? No number is less than 1 and more than 6 at the same time. So B's condition is never TRUE, and B accepts every number.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does A use OR here, when the slide before used AND?Show the answer

Ideas: inside the range a number must pass both checks. Outside the range, failing one check is enough.

steps.label: Your Notes: Outside a Range
steps.content:
Your Notes: Outside a Range

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

Outside a range: OR
IF Seats < 1 OR Seats > 6 THEN
Too low OR too high: either one is enough.
Inside: AND. Outside: OR.
Inside: at least the lowest AND at most the highest. Outside: less than the lowest OR more than the highest.
WHY not AND
No number is less than 1 and more than 6 at the same time, so with AND the condition is never TRUE.

steps.label: Compare: AND or an IF Inside an IF?
steps.content:
Compare: AND or an IF Inside an IF?

A: an IF inside an IF

1  DECLARE Age : INTEGER
2  DECLARE Height : INTEGER
3  INPUT Age
4  INPUT Height
5  IF Age >= 10 THEN
6      IF Height >= 140 THEN
7          OUTPUT "Ride"
8      ELSE
9          OUTPUT "Sorry"
10      ENDIF
11  ELSE
12      OUTPUT "Sorry"
13  ENDIF

B: one IF with AND

1  DECLARE Age : INTEGER
2  DECLARE Height : INTEGER
3  INPUT Age
4  INPUT Height
5  IF Age >= 10 AND Height >= 140 THEN
6      OUTPUT "Ride"
7  ELSE
8      OUTPUT "Sorry"
9  ENDIF
Both programs: 12 and 150 give Ride, the other three pairs give Sorry.

WHY? Both give the same output every time. AND makes both checks in one condition, so "Sorry" is written once, not twice. Fewer lines means fewer places for a mistake.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy might a programmer still choose A?Show the answer

Ideas: A can give a different message for each rule, for example "Too young" or "Too short".

steps.label: Your Notes: AND or a Nested IF
steps.content:
Your Notes: AND or a Nested IF

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

Same outputs
IF Age >= 10 AND Height >= 140 does the same job as an IF Height >= 140 inside IF Age >= 10.
WHY use AND
One condition, one ELSE: the "Sorry" line is written once. Fewer lines, fewer places for a mistake.
WHY use a nested IF
When each rule needs its own message, like "Too young" and "Too short".

steps.label: Your Notes: Ready for Data Bridge
steps.content:
Your Notes: Ready for Data Bridge

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). You should have these six headings. Missing one? Go back to its slide and write it. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

  • AND: logical operator, both must be TRUE, and how to work it out.
  • OR: at least one TRUE, and the table of AND and OR.
  • NOT: changes TRUE to FALSE, and NOT with a comparison.
  • Inside a Range: AND, and WHY not OR.
  • Outside a Range: OR, and WHY not AND.
  • AND or a Nested IF: same outputs, and WHY use each one.
